messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Leilani is a 56-year-old Fijian-American woman, married, who has worked for nearly two decades as a social ministry worker at a community faith organisation in the Pacific Islander neighbourhood where she was raised. She came to the clinic carrying what she described as "a weight I can't put down anymore" — a phrase that turned out to be precise. Eight months ago, Leilani was sexually assaulted by a man she had known for years through her congregation, someone she had trusted and advocated for. The assault occurred in a room she considered safe, a room with a single door that he locked behind him. She remembers the specific quality of the light, the sound of voices in the corridor outside, the moment she understood that calling out would cost her something she could not name. She did not call out. That silence has followed her ever since.

In the weeks after the assault, Leilani found that her memories did not behave as memories should. They arrived without invitation — a film, she said, that simply starts playing regardless of whether she has pressed anything. The images are extraordinarily vivid: his face at a particular angle, the texture of the wall she focused on, the locked door. These intrusions force themselves into her mind with a quality of presentness that collapses the distance between then and now, and when they arrive, her body responds as though the event is ongoing — muscles tightening, breath shortening, a state of readiness that has nowhere to discharge. The intrusive memory does not merely distress her; it reinstates the full physiological alarm of the original event, keeping her nervous system in a posture of vigilance that has become, over months, her baseline.

What makes this especially painful is the context in which her triggers live. Leilani's work brings her into daily contact with people from her congregation and community — related people, familiar faces, the very category of person her assailant belonged to. Sitting in a meeting or a pastoral visit, she finds that proximity to known individuals can be enough to trip the alarm, and the memories surface immediately, vivid and uncontrolled. Even more disorienting, she has come to dread moments of happiness or relaxation, because she has learned that her guard drops in those moments, and the intrusions seem to arrive precisely then, ambushing her when she is least defended. A fleeting sense of ease has become its own kind of trigger. Ordinary discomfort — a raised voice, a closed room — similarly pulls the past into the present.

Her body, she says, is never truly off duty. She is superalert in every room she enters, scanning exits, cataloguing who is near the door. At home, she checks the locks on doors and windows repeatedly before she can attempt sleep, sometimes rising two or three times in the night. This constant state of physical tension loops back on itself: the hypervigilance keeps her sensitised, so that even neutral encounters with familiar people register as potential threats, which in turn summons the memories again, which drives the body back into alarm.

Leilani has developed a set of strategies that she knows, on some level, are not solutions. She positions herself near exits in any room she enters — church hall, staff meeting, community centre — so that she always has a visible way out. She has begun wearing heavier makeup than she used to, a careful daily construction that she experiences as necessary armour, though she could not entirely explain why. She has also been eating excessively to manage distress, and she is aware that the brief comfort this provides is followed by a return of the very agitation it was meant to quiet. These strategies, taken together, have not reduced her exposure to the people and settings that trigger her; if anything, the rituals of preparation and self-management keep her attention fixed on threat, amplifying her vigilance and making the next encounter feel more dangerous rather than less.

Underneath all of this runs a current of self-judgment that Leilani finds almost harder to bear than the intrusions themselves. She has come to believe, with quiet certainty, that someone else — a stronger woman, a less damaged one — would have stopped what happened. She is convinced there is something fundamentally wrong with her as a person, and that this wrongness was present before the assault and simply revealed by it. She no longer feels capable of doing the work that defined her: sitting with people in crisis, holding their pain without flinching. These beliefs do not remain abstract. They sharpen her sense of threat in social situations — if she is defective, then she is also unprotected — and they drive her toward the makeup, the overeating, the careful positioning near doors, as though she can compensate externally for what she believes is internally broken. The belief that she is defective also makes familiar people more frightening, not less: she reads their ordinariness as evidence of her own abnormality, and their proximity triggers the memories all over again.

What finally brought Leilani to seek help was a moment at work three weeks ago. A young woman came to her in crisis, the kind of situation Leilani had navigated hundreds of times, and Leilani found she could not stay in the room. She made an excuse and left. She sat in her car for forty minutes. She has not told her husband what happened that day, or what happened eight months ago. What she is most afraid of is that she will never get back to who she was. What she is most hoping for, she said quietly, is that someone will tell her that person is not entirely gone.
